t.1.216.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed, the blessed Fire, the oblation-eater whose banner is smoke, called to mind Varuṇa, wishing to see him, that guardian of the world, the god born of Aditi who dwells in the waters, the lord of the waters.
t.1.216.2: And he, knowing what Pāvaka had thought of, showed himself to him. Having honored the lord of the waters, the great lord, the fourth of the world-guardians and their protector, Dhūmaketu spoke to him.
t.1.216.4: "For Pārtha will accomplish a very great task with the Gāṇḍīva, and Vāsudeva with the discus; therefore let that be given for my sake." "I shall give it," Varuṇa replied to Pāvaka.
t.1.216.3: The bow and the two quivers that King Soma gave to you, give both of them quickly, and also the chariot bearing the monkey emblem.
t.1.216.5: Then came that wondrous thing of great might, which increases fame and renown, unassailable by any weapon and crushing all weapons, the foremost of all arms, the overwhelmer of enemy hosts.
t.1.216.7: He gave that jewel of a bow, worshipped for endless years by the gods, Dānavas and Gandharvas, and also two great inexhaustible quivers.
t.1.216.6: It was matchless, equal to a hundred thousand bows, an increaser of kingdoms, variegated and adorned with colors high and low, smooth and without a flaw.
t.1.216.8: And a chariot yoked with divine horses, bearing a banner with the foremost of monkeys, furnished with silvery Gandharva steeds garlanded with gold, resembling pale-white clouds, equal in speed to mind and wind.
t.1.216.10: It was what Bhauvana, the Prajāpati and lord of the worlds, had created through his own austerity, and its form, like that of the sun, could not be described.
t.1.216.9: That chariot was furnished with every kind of equipment, invincible to the gods and Dānavas, radiant, of mighty thunderous roar, and captivating the minds of all beings.
t.1.216.11: It was the chariot which the lord Soma once mounted to conquer the Dānavas, resembling a mountain or a cloud and seeming to blaze with splendor.
t.1.216.14: On its banner there were creatures of many kinds, huge ones, at whose roar the senses of enemy armies are lost.
t.1.216.12: Fixed upon that best of chariots was a flagstaff, auspicious and like the weapon of Śakra, made of gold, exceedingly beautiful and unsurpassed.
t.1.216.13: Upon it a divine monkey, bearing the marks of a lion and a tiger, stood there firmly set at the top and shone, as though roaring.
t.1.216.15: He, having circumambulated, keeping it on his right, that excellent chariot adorned with various banners, and having bowed to the deities,
t.1.216.16: Armed and armored, bearing a sword, wearing his bound guards of iguana hide for arm and fingers, Pārtha mounted the chariot as a man of good deeds ascends a celestial vimāna.
t.1.216.17: Taking up that divine Gāṇḍīva, the best of bows, fashioned long ago by Brahmā, Arjuna was filled with delight.
t.1.216.18: Then the mighty one, having bowed to Hutāśana, summoning his strength, took up that bow as well and joined the bow with its string.
t.1.216.20: Having obtained the chariot and the bow, as well as the two great inexhaustible quivers, the son of Kuntī became ready and was delighted at the task of giving aid.
t.1.216.19: And as the bowstring was being fitted by the mighty Pāṇḍava, the minds of those who heard its twang there were truly shaken.
t.1.216.22: And Pāvaka said to him, "With this, O Madhusūdana, you will without doubt conquer in battle even beings who are not human."
t.1.216.21: Then Pāvaka gave Kṛṣṇa a discus with a hub of adamant, a beloved fiery weapon, and at that moment he too became ready for battle.
t.1.216.23: With this, you will always, without doubt, be superior in battle to men and even to gods, to Rakṣases, Piśācas, Daityas and Nāgas, in a battle that crushes the foremost of foes.
t.1.216.24: Each time this is hurled by you in battle against your enemies, O Mādhava, it will slay them unchecked in combat and return to your hand again.
t.1.216.25: And Varuṇa gave him a terrible mace that roared like the thunderbolt and brought destruction to the Daityas, the mace of Hari named Kaumodakī.
t.1.216.26: Then Kṛṣṇa and the Pāṇḍava, overjoyed, spoke to Pāvaka, the two of them now skilled in weapons, well furnished with arms, possessed of chariots and of banners as well.
t.1.216.27: O lord, we two are able to fight even with all the gods and asuras together; how much more, then, with the lone wielder of the thunderbolt, who is eager to fight for the sake of the serpent!
t.1.216.29: Taking up the bow Gāṇḍīva and likewise the two great inexhaustible quivers, I too am able, O Pāvaka, to conquer the worlds in battle.
t.1.216.28: When the mighty Vārṣṇeya hurls his discus as a weapon in battle, there is nothing in the three worlds that Janārdana could not conquer.
t.1.216.30: Surround it on all sides with a great forest fire, O lord, and blaze forth today as you wish; we two are ready for the work of helping you.
t.1.216.31: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Thus addressed by the Dāśārha and by Arjuna, the blessed lord assumed his fiery form and began to burn the forest.
t.1.216.32: Then the seven-flamed blazing Fire, enraged, surrounded the Khāṇḍava forest on all sides and burned it, as if displaying the end of the age.
t.1.216.33: Having seized that forest, O bull of the Bharatas, he entered it with a roar like the thundering of clouds, burning up all creatures.
t.1.216.34: As that forest burned, O Bhārata, its form shone forth like that of Meru, the lord of mountains, golden and of great splendor.
